title: Transposable elements and the evolutionary origins of C4 gene expression: The story of carbonic anhydrases in Flaveria
content: C4 photosynthesis is a CO2-concentrating mechanism that enhances photosynthetic efficiency in warm, dry, and open habitats. The C4 mechanism relies on a biochemical cycle that operates across two adjacent cell types, namely mesophyll (M) and bundle sheath (BS) cells. Atmospheric CO2 that enters the leaf is converted to bicarbonate (HCO3−) in M cells, where it is initially fixed into a C4 acid that diffuses to BS cells, which is the site of Rubisco (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) and Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle reactions in C4 plants. In BS cells, the decarboxylation of the C4 acid creates a high-CO2 environment that saturates Rubisco, suppressing its oxygenase activity and preventing carbon loss via photorespiration. As a result, C4 plants can sustain high carbon assimilation rates under CO2-limiting conditions, and this largely explains the ecological success of numerous C4 lineages in tropical and subtropical grasslands and savannas (Sage et al 2012).
